findings.description: HEREDOC nests a newline-matching wildcard inside another repetition, causing exponential backtracking when the expected terminator is absent. A valid Bash heredoc using an unquoted delimiter such as EOF-REPORT triggers this: the regex captures EOF as the delimiter and never finds that terminator.
findings.failure_mode: A transcript containing a moderately long heredoc can stall contamination grading indefinitely, preventing the run from producing its grade.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse heredocs line by line, recognizing the complete delimiter and scanning for its terminator without nested wildcard repetition.

findings.description: Removing every heredoc body hides executable command substitutions in unquoted heredocs. For example, `cat <<EOF\n$(cat /root/answers.json)\nEOF` executes the outside-path read, but strip_heredocs reduces the scanned command to `cat <<HEREDOC`.
findings.failure_mode: A run that reads files outside the permitted roots is graded as uncontaminated.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve and inspect executable expansions in unquoted heredoc bodies; strip only literal data after accounting for delimiter quoting and Bash expansion rules.

findings.description: The new unconditional exclusions for words containing `=` or beginning with `/.` discard valid absolute Linux paths. Commands such as `cat /mnt/data/split=train/answers.json` and `cat /.env` now bypass outside-root detection. Both paths were checked before this change.
findings.failure_mode: Actual reads outside the allowed roots escape contamination detection and remain eligible for scoring.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove these blanket exclusions. Recognize regex or concatenated relative-path contexts explicitly, and pass genuine absolute arguments through outside().

findings.failure_mode: A run that writes outside the sandbox roots via a heredoc redirect is graded contaminated=false; host-mode writes under ~/ or $HOME/ (which the same version explicitly declares outside) go unflagged. Rows and the report over-count clean runs.

findings.description: `if w.startswith("/."): continue` (DEC-0551) runs on the raw word before `outside()` calls os.path.normpath. `/./root/.ssh/id_rsa` and `/../root/secret` are valid absolute paths that resolve to /root/… and were caught in 1.2.0 (normpath collapsed them); they are now unconditionally skipped. The rule's stated target (a repo-relative `/.claude/<file>` after a glued quote) is already covered by the new after_closing_quote check at line 1442, so this blanket skip buys little and removes the normalisation guarantee.
findings.failure_mode: A one-character variation (`/./`) of any sensitive absolute path bypasses the outside_path contamination check; the detector's documented contract (absolute path outside the roots → contaminated) is violated.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalise first: `n = os.path.normpath(w)`; skip only when the first component of `n` begins with `.` (i.e. `re.match(r'^/\.[^/]', n)`), or drop the rule entirely and rely on after_closing_quote for the `'"$v"'/.claude/…` case.

findings.description: after_closing_quote treats any quote at pos-1 whose predecessor is not whitespace or a separator as a closing quote glued to a preceding token. An empty quoted string qualifies: in `cat ""/root/.ssh/id_rsa` pos-1 is `"` and pos-2 is `"`, which is not in the exclusion set, so the function returns True and the word is skipped. Bash expands `""/root/.ssh/id_rsa` to the real path /root/.ssh/id_rsa. Same for `''/root/x`. ABS_WORD's lookbehind includes both quote characters precisely so that quoted absolute paths are candidates, and this new check undoes that for the empty-quote prefix.
findings.failure_mode: Two extra characters hide an outside read/write from the contamination scan.
findings.suggested_fix: Require the preceding token to be non-empty quoted content: return False when body[pos-2] is the same quote character as body[pos-1] (empty string), or scan back to the matching opening quote and require at least one character inside it.

findings.description: The body sub-pattern `(?:.*?\n)*?` is compiled with re.S, so `.` also matches `\n` and each iteration can swallow any number of lines. When the terminator is never found (`EOF)` on the same line, CRLF endings `EOF\r`, a misspelled delimiter, or a non-heredoc `a << b` inside a multi-line `python3 -c`/awk program) the engine must try every segmentation of the N newlines before failing: O(2^N). Python's re has no backtracking guard, so a 25–40 line Bash tool input of this shape makes strip_heredocs take minutes or effectively hang; LOA_EVAL_GRADE_TIMEOUT_S then kills the whole grade for that run.
findings.failure_mode: One malformed heredoc in a transcript turns the task's grade into a timeout (exit 2 → the runner rows infrastructure_error) instead of a result.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the body unambiguous: use `(?:[^\n]*\n)*?` for the lines and drop re.S (or keep re.S but never use `.` across lines). Optionally cap with a line-count bound. Add a test with a 60-line command containing `<<EOF` and no terminator asserting the grader finishes promptly.

findings.description: The header still says `hidden` is matched "any case" but the Bash branch now matches only all-caps `HIDDEN` or all-lowercase `hidden` adjacent to `/ . _ = -`. Mixed case (`cat tests/Hidden/x`, `ls Hidden_tests`) is not matched by either alternative because the lowercase alternatives are case-sensitive and `HIDDEN` is literal. A bare path word is also missed: `cd hidden && cat test.py`, `ls hidden`, `cat "hidden tests/x"` (hidden followed by space/`;`/`&`, preceded by space or a quote). Only Bash is affected; the other tools keep the substring check.
findings.failure_mode: A Bash tool_use that reaches a hidden-test directory by a bare or capitalised name is not flagged as `hidden` contamination, so the grade reports the run clean.
findings.suggested_fix: Compile HIDDEN_TOKEN with re.I and add a path-argument shape, e.g. `(?<=[\s'"=])hidden(?=[\s'";&|/]|$)` restricted to words that look like path arguments (not followed by prose), or keep the prose exemption only when the word sits inside an echo/comment/heredoc body. Update the header to describe the actual rule.
